# Boolean operation {#sec-boolean-operation}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Q: Lahy sa vavy ny zanakao? A: Eny
:::

The statement above is a joke between two logicians (the branch of mathematics that study boolean variables). But almost nobody laughs about it and barely grin when explained. Operations with numbers are natural @sec-numeric and @sec-arithmetic. However those on logical/boolean variables @sec-boolean are less intuitive. Imagine the boolean variable below (which also called statement or propositio)

A: Radama is a male --TRUE
B: Radama is Malagasy -- TRUE

C: Ranavalona is a male -- FALSE
D: Ranavalona is Malagasy -- TRUE

The operation with boolean is when we combine P1 and P2,

P1: A AND B means Radama is a male AND Radama is Malagasy.
P1 is TRUE, and formally: TRUE AND TRUE = TRUE

P2: A OR B: Radama a male OR Radama is Malagasy
P2 is also TRUE, Formally: TRUE OR TRUE = TRUE

P3: C AND D: Ranavalona is male AND Ranavalona is Malagasy.
P3 is FALSE so FALSE AND TRUE = FALSE

And the final combination
P4: C OR D: Ranavalona is male OR Ranavalona is Malagasy.
P4 is TRUE so FALSE OR TRUE = TRUE

Back to the joke above. The question could be reframed as two statement
Statement 1: Your new born is a male
Statement 2: Your new born is a female
Statement 1 OR statement 2 is always TRUE because one of them must be TRUE.

Boolean operation are fundamental parts of programming and can be quite unintuitive (as with the joke for the untrained). While they is reserved to logician. It is essential to become literate. Concrete examples of application are shown in the tips section below.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
The AND is encoded as `&` in R `A & B` or `A && B`
The OR is encoded as `|` in R as `A | B` or `A || B`

Ths double is mainly for short-circuit used in loop
Single is for filtering.

A final symbol is `!` whic is used for negation. So `!A` is the opposite of `A`


## Examples {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| echo: true

a <- TRUE
b <- TRUE
cc <- FALSE

a | b
a & b
a & cc

a | (b & cc)
(a | b) & cc

# examples with negation
!a


```

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- These boolean operator are also the same as intersection (AND) and union (OR).
- Boolean operators are crucial when you want to filter data. Each statement is a criteria included in the data Imaging one survey 100 people and recored their nationality and sex. To filter data say just male and malagasy you apply boolean operator AND. If one collect tree and select of a certain dbh and and a given species dbh > 30 && species == "Dalbergia" or add a third criteria
- One might need to use parentheses as results will differ
- Why double or single symbol?
- Logic is at the base of mathematics. It is the fundamental and as such it could be the most mental. We just what we need.
